newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Business gives Hong Kong '97 budget mixed reviews.
newsitem.headline: Business gives Hong Kong '97 budget mixed reviews.

text.p: Hong Kong's transitional budget won mixed reviews from the territory's business community on Wednesday, many of whom expected Financial Secretary Donald Tsang to cut already-low tax rates.

Some hailed the government's decision to sit on a huge cash pile as prudent strategy in a year of momentous change, but others said the territory could well afford tax cuts to signal strong confidence in its future and improve competitiveness.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule. The 1997/98 budget will straddle the handover, just 111 days away.

"The 1997/98 budget always had the potential to be a difficult one, but consultation and cooperation (with China) has produced a result conservative in its approach, but acceptable to most in the community," said the chairman of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, James Tien.
Tien said the budget was well-executed and a "sound basis for confidence".

Tsang resisted temptation to cut taxes despite a 1996/97 (April-March) budget surplus of HK$15.1 billion ($1.95 billion) and total fiscal reserves, including land fund revenues, estimated at HK$330 billion by the time Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control on July 1 this year.

Hong Kong's budget surpluses are expected to continue rising after the handover. A surplus of HK$31.7 billion is forecast at March 31, 1998 with a combined surplus of HK$58.9 billion forecast for the three fiscal years of 1998/99 to 2000/01.

"I would like to see the government take a more pro-active role in maintaining Hong Kong's position of pre-eminence and competitiveness as a regional and international business, financial and services centre," said KPMG Peat Marwick tax partner Jennifer Wong.

Rather than issuing an across-the-board tax cut advocated by some experts, Tsang opted for a collection of moves involving personal allowances and tax bands which, he said, would benefit 96 percent of the tax-paying public.
"It is consistent with all previous budgets...there has been no significant change in tax rates, tax concessions," said Rod Houng-Lee, head of taxation at Price Waterhouse.
In spending estimates announced earlier, the government also stuck firmly to its principle of restricting spending to less than 20 percent of gross domestic product.
This would keep government spending increases firmly in line with a long-term economic growth rate of five percent.

Rejecting allegations of Beijing budgetary pressure to restrict spending and resist tax cuts, Tsang also warned that volatile revenues which generated Hong Kong's stellar wealth this year could not be relied upon in the future.

Stamp duty, a lucrative transactions tax on the territory's booming property and stock markets, yielded bumper returns in the latter stages of the current fiscal year, Tsang said, boosting revenue by an unexpected HK$6.6 billion.

"While additional revenue is always welcome, these increases come from two particularly volatile sources. It would not be wise for me to anticipate that this boost to our finances would be maintained over the medium term," Tsang said.
Tsang also warned that huge capital expenditures will be necessary in the next few years and will eat into any surpluses.
Marshall Byres, chairman of taxation at Ernst & Young, dismissed this reasoning.

"He's used this as a pretence, it's the only word I can use, as the rationale for keeping all this money, which is clearly what Beijing consultants who were in this group wanted him to do," Byres said.

The 1997/98 budget was drawn up in cooperation with China, which now must stand back and allow Hong Kong to run its own financial affairs under the Basic Law, the constitution promulgated by China to govern Hong Kong following the handover.
($ = 7.74 HK dollars)
